title: Inference on the Value of Policy Improvement in Adaptive Experiments
abstract: In this paper, we develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data. This value, which is defined as the gap between the value of the best treatment policy in a class and that of a baseline policy, gauges whether or not it is worth deploying a personalized treatment policy. Building an estimator for the VPI is naturally more difficult than estimating the value of a fixed policy. This is because, in addition to contending with the correlated data and decaying propensities associated with adaptive experiments, any estimator must also handle the non-regularity, or lack of pathwise differentiability, of the underlying estimand when the optimal policy is non-unique. Our proposed estimator works by sequentially fitting a weighted empirical welfare maximizing policy on historical data and then evaluating it using inverse propensity weighting on future samples. We neither assume that the optimal policy is unique nor make a margin assumption on the underlying heterogeneous treatment effects. A key difficulty in analyzing our estimator is showing that the regret incurred through policy learning is asymptotically smaller than the standard error of the estimator. We accomplish this by showing faster regret rates for policy learning under decaying propensities, which may be of independent interest. We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.

title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.

title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
abstract:
Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines.
  A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.

title: Who Sets the Pace of Judge Hacking? Judge Capability versus the Policy-Judge Gap
abstract: When a policy is trained with GRPO against a frozen, reference-free LLM judge, the judge accepts more of its answers, but in a post-hoc analysis we detect no gain in held-out greedy accuracy: in all 12 (policy, judge) cells, the seed-mean gain never exceeded 0.04. A gold-reward control with the same recipe raised the 1.5B policy's greedy accuracy by +0.054 [0.013, 0.096], so for this policy the flat accuracy is specific to the judge reward; for the 0.5B policy, gold reward also gave no detectable gain. In the four rising cells we checked, the early rise in training-rollout accuracy is mostly sampling sharpening, as it is under gold reward. We then ask whether the policy-judge gap or the judge sets how far and how fast RL exploits the judge's false positives. We train 0.5B and 1.5B Qwen2.5 policies against four judges at least as large (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B, Llama-3.2-3B) and the 1.5B policy against one smaller judge (Qwen3-0.6B). The depth of judge hacking (the plateau) tracks the judge: it correlates with judge AUC (Spearman -0.69 [-0.94, -0.14] over 12 cells), and within a family the larger judge is fooled less deeply. For the pace (onset), two pre-specified pairs contradict the gap account (the larger-gap cell was fooled 3.5x sooner at the pre-specified threshold). With 12 cells we cannot formally separate judge AUC from the gap for either endpoint. The smaller judge was not fooled sooner than a judge as large as the policy, though it also differs in family and template. In a blind test on three held-out judges, a hash-locked step-0 predictor did not beat step-0 AUC, but three cells cannot separate them. At 7-8B, judges from three families plateaued at 0.37, 0.67 and 0.85.

title: RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution
abstract: Recent focus in agentic reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to improve credit assignment in long-horizon tasks. One promising direction combines reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), integrating trajectory-level advantages with dense token-level supervision. This line of work often conditions a teacher model on privileged context, such as agentic skills, to score tokens generated by the student policy. Despite their progress, they largely overlook the on-policy evolution of agentic skills and the reliability of teacher supervision. Towards this end, we introduce Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization (RSIPO), a self-evolving agentic RL framework that enables agentic skills and the policy model to co-evolve throughout the training process. Specifically, RSIPO enables the policy itself to extract skills from completed trajectories and explicitly optimizes its skill-generation capability through trajectory replay. It further employs empirical Bayes shrinkage to dynamically calibrate the student's trust in teacher scores, accounting for the fact that skill-enhanced teacher guidance can sometimes be less reliable. Experiments with Qwen-family models on embodied interaction and search-based agentic tasks demonstrate that RSIPO outperforms all the compared baseline approaches. With Qwen2.5-7B as the base model, RSIPO achieves an average success rate of 98.6\% on ALFWorld, yielding absolute improvements of 2.5\% and 17.4\% over the second-best baseline and standard GRPO, respectively.

title: Robust Marathi Sentiment Analysis using Domain-Adaptive Pre-training and Data Augmentation Approaches
abstract: For languages with limited resources, Sentiment Analysis remains a challenging problem due to limited annotated data and strong domain variability across textual sources. Marathi, despite being widely spoken, lacks extensive multi-domain sentiment analysis studies. Recent efforts by L3Cube have introduced multi-domain datasets in Marathi, enabling a better study of domain-aware sentiment classification. This study uses the pretrained MahaBERT model to improve sentiment classification for Marathi across different domains. Models are trained on individual domain datasets and domain-adaptive pretraining is applied using masked language modeling to help the model better understand domain-specific language. In addition, back-translation is used as a method of data augmentation to increase the diversity of training data. Results show that these methods lead to consistent improvements in accuracy across all domains. The improvements range from a minimum of about 0.12% to a maximum of about 1.74%, depending on the dataset. These results demonstrate that domain-adaptive pretraining and data augmentation are effective strategies for improving sentiment analysis models. This helps achieve more robust performance across different domains and makes the approach more suitable for low-resource languages like Marathi.

title: Hyperbolic Time Series Forecasting with Learnable Decomposition and Manifold Dynamics
abstract: Multiscale structure is central to time series forecasting: temporal signals contain slowly varying trends, intermediate seasonal patterns, and high-frequency residuals. Traditional forecasters model this multiscale structure in Euclidean space, without representing the ordering it induces among components. We identify that cascaded decomposition orders components by their characteristic frequencies, forming a natural frequency hierarchy. This hierarchy aligns with the exponential volume growth of hyperbolic space, which provides increasing representational capacity with radius and naturally accommodates nested hierarchies. We propose HyperForecast, the first long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) framework operating in hyperbolic space. HyperForecast embeds decomposed temporal segments on the Poincaré ball where radial distance captures this nested structure, from low-frequency components near the origin to high-frequency components near the boundary. We model geodesic velocity through two manifold-dynamics variants: (a) autoregressive forecasting via Poincaré residual dynamics, and (b) non-autoregressive forecasting that predicts all future segments in parallel. HyperForecast consistently outperforms existing and state-of-the-art baselines on 9 of 11 long-term forecasting benchmarks, achieving up to 58% lower mean squared error at long horizons. Further analysis reveals that the learned radial embeddings recover the frequency hierarchy and that hyperbolic geometry contributes substantially to forecasting performance.

title: Enhancing Zero-Shot Domain Transfer in Low-Resource Sentiment Analysis: A Case Study in Marathi
abstract: Sentiment analysis is a key task in Natural Language Processing that determines the polarity of opinions in text. For low-resource languages like Marathi--where limited data prevents the direct use of standard statistical methods--models are often trained on single-domain datasets. While this yields strong in-domain performance, it leads to poor generalization to unseen domains. Recent studies highlight the need for domain-robust systems that can handle diverse real-world content through multi-domain modeling. This study investigates how multi-domain training improves sentiment classification for unseen Marathi domains. Models are trained using single-domain, two-domain, and three-domain dataset combinations. Results show that two-domain training improves accuracy on unseen domains by about 8\% compared to single-domain training. Adding a third domain provides further improvement, though the gain is smaller, averaging around 2\% for some domains. These results suggest that training with data from multiple domains helps build more robust sentiment analysis models for low-resource languages, though the benefits reduce as more domains are added.

title: NepPlural: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Persona Annotation in Nepali Migration Discourse
abstract: Pluralistic alignment asks that language models faithfully represent a society's diverse, competing values rather than collapse them into one dominant viewpoint, yet flagship pluralistic-alignment datasets remain heavily skewed toward Western respondents. We introduce NepPlural, a human-anchored benchmark for modelling competing socio-cultural personas in Nepali public discourse on youth migration and brain drain. We curate 2,148 code-mixed (Devanagari, Romanized Nepali, English) YouTube comments, annotate them along a four-axis persona taxonomy (Intent, Primary Driver, Value Orientation, Affect) plus an explicit No-Persona class, and build a 300-comment gold set labelled independently by three native Nepali speakers (mean Fleiss' $κ\approx 0.55$). Using this gold set to audit automatic annotation, we find that LLM annotation reliability is driven by protocol. Labels collected in batches through chat interfaces reach only near-chance inter-model agreement ($κ\approx 0.17$). Annotating one comment at a time raises agreement above the native-speaker level ($κ\approx 0.72$), but consistency is not validity: under a forced-choice schema, models agree on personas for the 39% of comments native speakers judge to express none, keeping macro-F1 against human gold near 0.50. Allowing abstention resolves this: models recover No-Persona comments with F1 of 0.79 to 0.87 and, against leave-one-annotator-out references, match or exceed individual native speakers (macro-F1 0.75 to 0.86 vs. 0.75). Encoders fine-tuned on the batched labels reach only 0.34. Finally, a human-judged steerability probe finds that three frontier models adopt single persona axes with 59 to 77% fidelity but compose full personas only 33% of the time, with no congruence gap detected at this scale between Western-congruent and Nepali-collectivist personas.

title: A Dependency-Aware Multi-GPU Training Framework for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) achieve superior performance in many dynamic graph learning tasks. These models use node state vectors (i.e., memories) to capture and record graph changes (i.e., events), and then exploit these memories to assist prediction. However, this memory-centric design makes multi-GPU training challenging because predictions for later events often depend on memory updates from earlier events. To maintain model quality, existing multi-GPU TGNN training schemes strictly preserve all event dependencies, which limits parallelism and causes expensive cross-GPU memory synchronization. In this work, we observe that many of these dependencies can be handled more flexibly without harming training quality. Specifically, (a) dependencies in TGNN training have high locality in both time and graph topology, (b) the short-range dependencies missed within a large batch can often be recovered cheaply, and (c) many memory updates are not immediately needed. Based on these observations, we propose DepBloom to accelerate multi-GPU TGNN training with three techniques: (1) temporally bounded spatial partitioning to reduce unnecessary cross-GPU synchronization and improve parallelism; (2) intra-batch memory refinement to recover missing short-range temporal dependencies inside enlarged batches; and (3) critical-path optimization to prioritize urgent memory updates while deferring non-critical work during multi-GPU pipeline execution. Experimental results across representative models and diverse datasets show that DepBloom achieves an average speedup of 2.84$\times$ and up to 5.16$\times$ over state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining comparable or better model accuracy.

title: Uncovering the Generative Landscape of Diffusion Models: A Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion Framework
abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have emerged as powerful generative priors across domains ranging from molecular design to high-resolution image synthesis. However, standard diffusion sampling is inherently biased toward high-likelihood regions, often limiting the diversity of outputs. In many domains, a single, high-likelihood sample is insufficient. Instead, diverse portfolios of high-performing solutions are required, motivating methods that uncover a model's full expressive range. Here we show that integrating Quality-Diversity (QD) optimisation with diffusion models enables the discovery of diverse, high-performing outputs. We first propose Quality-Diversity Diffusion, a framework that adapts QD to diffusion models by directly optimising the model's latent noise and conditioning embeddings and leveraging embedding models to quantify diversity. Second, we introduce a novel h-space Spectral Mutation operator, which guides search along directions of maximal semantic sensitivity by analysing principal singular vectors of the model's input-to-activation Jacobian. We evaluate our combined approach, Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion, on text-to-image generation. Against 12 baselines, our method consistently achieves the lowest FID score, demonstrating an excellent balance of image quality and diversity.

title: Adaptive Robust Confidence Sets in High Dimensions
abstract:
We study adaptive confidence sets for mean vectors of multivariate Gaussians with identity covariance under Huber contamination when the contamination proportion is unknown. We show that an information-theoretically optimal adaptive confidence set can be constructed by simultaneously quantifying uncertainty across all one-dimensional projections. The resulting confidence set achieves the optimal diameter and reveals a substantial adaptation cost compared with the minimax estimation error.
  Although statistically optimal, this construction is computationally infeasible. We establish a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound showing that achieving diameter $O(m^{-1/2})$ requires either exponentially many queries or query tolerance $d^{-Ω(m)}$. Thus, in contrast to robust mean estimation, adaptation to the unknown contamination proportion incurs both a statistical cost and a computational barrier within the SQ framework.
  Finally, we give a low-degree moment-matching algorithm that constructs an adaptive confidence set using $d^{O(m)}$ samples and time. Its diameter bound contains an additional $O(m^{-1/2})$ term beyond the information-theoretic rate, matching the dependence on $m$ in the SQ lower bound. Together, these results characterize the statistical limits of adaptive robust confidence sets under Huber contamination and quantify a computational barrier within the SQ framework.

title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
abstract: Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver's native safety behavior as safety incompatibility. Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo, a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.

title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.

title: TL;QR: Querying Temporal Discursive Patterns in Textual Corpora
abstract: Many questions about large textual corpora concern patterns that unfold over time, such as a political group whose stance on a topic drifts from support to criticism over several years of debates. We present TL;QR (Too Long; Query with logical temporal Reasoning), a declarative query language and open-source engine for finding such temporal discursive patterns. In TL;QR, a single query combines natural-language predicates, whose truth is judged by a Large Language Model (LLM), with regular expressions and the operators of a temporal logic. The LLM answers only local questions about individual text passages; a symbolic engine then aggregates these judgments over time and links every match to the recorded passages and predicate decisions behind it. With this division of labor, the temporal and relational reasoning stays exact and auditable even over long time horizons. In addition, when a query includes a regular-expression pre-filter, only a small fraction of the corpus ever reaches the LLM. On a suite of controlled synthetic benchmarks with temporally and semantically complex patterns, TL;QR is substantially more accurate than LLM-only baselines. In a case study on ten years of European Parliament debates (442,593 multilingual speeches), TL;QR identifies candidate shifts in the political groups' stances on the GDPR privacy regulation.

title: What DNA Foundation Models Learn Beyond Sequence Composition
abstract: Do genomic foundation models (FMs) provide predictive information beyond simple sequence composition? We evaluate frozen representations from five DNA FMs against normalized k-mer frequencies across 57 genomic classification datasets and two exploratory gene-expression regression tasks. Simple k-mer features remain competitive with most models, whereas NTv3 shows a consistent advantage; the ranking is robust to globally fixed and multi-scale k-mer baselines and alternative downstream probes. To test incremental predictive utility directly, we compare global 6-mer features with their concatenation with each FM embedding under a matched Random Forest protocol. NTv3 improves 46 of 57 datasets (mean $Δ$MCC = +0.072), while Caduceus provides smaller gains and the other models do not improve mean MCC. We separately decompose embeddings into a component linearly predictable from 6-mer frequencies and a ridge residual, finding that linear recoverability does not reliably indicate downstream utility. Exact 6-mer-preserving shuffles further reveal task-relevant sequence-order sensitivity, most pronounced for NTv3, although order sensitivity alone does not guarantee predictive improvements. Our results establish compositional features as essential controls and offer complementary diagnostics for evaluating the added value of frozen genomic representations, without making claims about fine-tuning capacity.

title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.

title: Generalizable Model Editing Could Be More Than Direct Generalization
abstract: A central desideratum in model editing is generalization to complex tasks, which prior work formalizes under a direct generalization paradigm: treating and evaluating LLM behavior as an input-output mapping and expecting a factual update to alter outputs on reasoning tasks. Yet despite substantial empirical effort, the field consensus remains that such generalization is highly challenging and elusive. However, when we deploy the latest models in an in-the-wild chatbot-user setting, we surprisingly find that even classical editing methods exhibit remarkably fluent generalization behavior. This motivates us to revisit the obstacles to generalization and the limitations of the prevailing paradigm. We find that direct generalization is fundamentally constrained both theoretically and practically: theoretically, it suffers from an identifiability issue; and practically, existing approaches attempting to circumvent this are further hindered by the ambiguity of their constructed biases and by vulnerability to being overridden by other factors such as optimization dynamics. We instead identify compositional generalization, empowered by the increasingly strong reasoning and composition abilities of modern LLMs, as a theoretically grounded and empirically validated alternative. We validate this phenomenon across multiple models and editing methods, showing that such generalization behavior is widespread. Overall, we argue that generalizable model editing could be more than direct generalization, and call for a paradigm shift toward more generalizable and practically deployable knowledge update techniques.

title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
abstract: India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.

title: RespFocus: Learning Temporal Evidence for Weakly Supervised Respiratory Sound Classification
abstract: Respiratory auscultation provides a low-cost means of assessing pulmonary function, yet transient crackles and sustained wheezes can be difficult to recognize in noisy clinical recordings. Conventional deep learning classifiers often operate as black boxes, offering limited insight into the temporal acoustic evidence supporting their predictions. We present RespFocus, a weakly supervised framework that uses multiple instance learning (MIL) to learn inspectable temporal evidence from cycle-level labels and integrate it into classification. We also introduce PedResp2026, a multicenter pediatric respiratory sound cohort collected in routine clinical environments with adjudicated cycle-level annotations. In classification experiments, RespFocus achieves four-class Scores of 69.55\% on public ICBHI 2017 and 72.91\% on PedResp2026. Evidence diagnostics and matched temporal interventions support the functional contribution of the learned evidence to model predictions. Together, these findings highlight RespFocus's potential as a tool for automated respiratory sound diagnosis.

title: TabMosaic: Unified In-Context Diffusion for Tabular Generative Tasks
abstract: Generative modeling for tabular data has advanced to the point where models can synthesize realistic records, recover missing values, and generate samples conditioned on class labels or observed attributes. Despite recent advances, existing approaches either require table-specific training or restrict in-context learning to single-cell prediction. In this work, we formulate these tabular generative tasks as a single problem: modeling the joint conditional distribution of an arbitrary set of target cells given the observed cells of an unseen table. To this end, we turn to diffusion, whose denoising objective is defined jointly over all target cells rather than one cell at a time. Under the pretraining distribution, this objective is minimized by the posterior predictive distribution over the target set. Building on this, we propose TabMosaic, a unified in-context diffusion model for generating mixed-type target cells in unseen, potentially incomplete tables without table-specific training. We further show that its pretraining objective bounds the conditional negative log-likelihood and the divergence from the posterior predictive for arbitrary target sets, extending the Bayesian account of in-context learning from a single-value prediction to joint multi-cell generation. Across 48 real-world tables, TabMosaic ranks first on all evaluated generative tasks against 20 baseline approaches

title: DRanker: A Transformer-Based Multi-Task Ranking Model for the Disney+ Homepage
abstract: We present DRanker (Disney+ Ranker), a transformer-based multitask ranking model serving personalized recommendations on the Disney+ homepage. We describe the encoder-only architecture over enriched engagement-history sequences paired with a lightweight causal debiasing mechanism, and the inference stack that enables transformer-based ranking at scale. Through iterative development, we systematically evaluated more complex alternatives and found that simpler designs consistently outperformed them on offline metrics, qualitative behavioral evaluation, and in production. Deployed globally, DRanker drives over 1% lift in our key engagement metric and 0.5% lift in daily active users across all experiences powered by the ranker. We share practical lessons on data engineering, debiasing, and architectural choices that shaped our ranking system at scale.

title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. We argue that progress requires validat- ing the interfaces between tutoring stages, not only improving individual components.

abstract: We establish uniform score bounds and Lipschitz continuity for truncated Gaussian, Cauchy, Boltzmann, and softmax policies under explicitly stated parameterizations.

title: When do explicit penalties improve flow matching?
abstract: Flow matching can learn structure directly from data, raising the question of when additional constraints improve generation. We study penalties that encode such constraints, with physics-informed flow matching as a motivating example. Satisfying a constraint more closely need not make the generated distribution more accurate. We therefore compare penalised and unpenalised generative modelling through their expected squared $2$-Wasserstein error. Our analysis covers both vector-valued and functional data in a Hilbert-space setting. We first derive geometric criteria that account for constraint violations and the distribution of samples after projection onto the constraint set. We then solve the statistical comparison explicitly for specific velocity-field classes and constraints via flow matching. In this model, penalisation improves accuracy exactly when the reduction in estimation variance outweighs the increase in squared bias. The resulting formula shows how this trade-off depends on sample size, the model class, the noise schedule, and the penalty weight.

title: Towards Autopilot Labeling for Short Video Content Governance
abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. In the L3 stage, we propose an agentic annotation workflow, and equip the agent with several key tools, which empower the agent to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases, significantly reducing the need for human intervention. We conduct extensive experiments across various content issues, and results demonstrate that each stage of the autopilot labeling framework progressively improves labeling accuracy, and has significantly reduced manual labor costs in real-world applications by up to 85%.

title: The Mathematical Collective Unconscious: Jungian Archetypes within the Latent Space
abstract: Carl Jung theorised that the human psyche contains an inherited framework, the collective unconscious, populated by universal archetypes. As large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast corpora of textual data, this paper investigates whether they spontaneously construct distinct archetype-like regions within their high-dimensional latent spaces. The paper proposes that these regions function as spatial constraints that naturally organise semantically related narratives. To evaluate this, we applied cosine similarity and angular distance metrics across thirteen experiments utilising OpenAIs text-embedding-3-small model. The paper contains two experimental sections the first section explores these ideas using synthetically constructed narratives, the results of which act as a baselines for experiments conducted in the second section where the synthetic data is replaced by human-authored literature (Shmoop corpus), unedited dream reports (DreamBank corpus), and culturally distilled folklore (Andrew Langs Fairy Books). The results show that archetypal roles occupy distinct, measurable regions in the latent space. Crucially, these regions remain compact and consistent because of narrative structure rather than simple word overlap. Additionally, text category dictates spatial distribution: dream reports concentrate within Trickster and Shadow regions, while traditional folklore distributes evenly across all tested archetypes. We conclude that transformer latent spaces encode stable regions which appear to correspond to recognised Jungian archetypes.

title: ProtoPur: Prototype-Purity Pseudo-Labeling for Weakly Supervised Instance Learning in Pathology
abstract: Weak bag-level labels are widely available in computational pathology, whereas reliable instance-level annotations for whole-slide images remain expensive and ambiguous. Weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) achieves strong bag-level classification, but instance-level supervision from attention scores, model predictions, negative bags, or spatial refinement may fail to identify class-specific local evidence. We propose ProtoPur, a prototype-purity pseudo-labeling method for weakly supervised instance-level learning in pathology whole-slide images. ProtoPur estimates class-balanced local purity over prototype regions constructed from frozen foundation-model features, and assigns pseudo-labels to high-purity regions strongly associated with a target class. This purity-first design separates class-specific evidence from negative or shared morphology, with coverage used only to ensure sufficient pseudo-label assignment. We provide a PAC-style analysis showing that the risk of an instance classifier trained with ProtoPur pseudo-labels can be decomposed into a standard uniform-convergence term and a ProtoPur-specific pseudo-label noise term, comprising selected-region mismatch and a coverage residual. Experiments on three public whole-slide image datasets with two pathology foundation encoders show that ProtoPur consistently improves instance-level performance across multiple MIL backbones while maintaining competitive bag-level performance. Pseudo-label quality comparisons on two public datasets further demonstrate that prototype-purity selection provides stronger instance supervision. These results suggest that the foundation-model features contain exploitable instance-level supervision signals, and ProtoPur is a way to reveal and use these signals from weak bag labels without requiring dense instance annotations.

title: Rate-Resolved Text Evaluation with Masked Diffusion Language Models
abstract: A single evaluation score can rank generation systems but rarely reveals what failed. We propose rate-resolved text evaluation, which turns the masking rate of masked diffusion language models into a diagnostic axis. By reconstructing text under different fractions of masked tokens, one diffusion score becomes a vector of band-conditioned scores that reflect reconstruction difficulty at varying levels of visible context. On SummEval, preserving this rate structure yields complementary signal: the best masking-rate band improves fusion with autoregressive likelihood over a collapsed diffusion scalar, survives a sample-shuffle control that breaks rate ordering, and adds residual signal to a fixed prompted judge. A second diffusion model reproduces the effect more weakly. On WMT MQM zh-en, roundtrip mask-and-reconstruct probing produces a tunable localization curve in which ranking-oriented AUROC and span-detection F1 peak at different masking rates. Factuality benchmarks bound the interpretation: band semantics are model- and task-dependent, so each application requires empirical validation.

title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.

title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

title: Feedback as an Interface: Controlling Form and Detail in LLM Translation Refinement
abstract: Feedback presentation shapes how LLMs use evaluator judgments during translation refinement. We introduce a machine translation protocol that keeps the evaluator score, main issue, and recommendation fixed while varying feedback form and supporting detail. Across seven models and six translation directions, low-load feedback outperforms high-load feedback in all 42 translator-direction settings under xCOMET. On the 29,400-record rewriting subset, mean xCOMET scores multiplied by 100 are 83.30 for low-load feedback and 80.67 for high-load feedback; the full-matrix original-translation reference mean is 83.46. MetricX-24 supports the low-load advantage on a stratified subset. A no-feedback second pass yields a small improvement over the original translations, and direct evaluator prompting reproduces the low-load advantage without a separate rewriting stage. These results show that compact feedback limits the quality loss from evaluator-guided refinement in the evaluated high-resource MT settings.

title: Testing Central Structure for Complex Networks
abstract: Centrality measures rank nodes even when the observed differences can be explained by ordinary structural variation. We therefore study a preceding question: whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all. We formulate this question as a network-level hypothesis testing issue using the adjacency spectral radius as the test statistic and estimate an empirical p-value from randomized networks generated under a specified null model. The framework is evaluated using G(N,M), Chung-Lu, and two implementations of the configuration model on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks. Controlled experiments further vary the number and connection weights of designated central nodes while holding network size and density fixed. The results show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the empirical p-value. They also demonstrate that rejection decisions depend substantially on the structural properties preserved by the null model: the detected network sets are not simply nested across models.
relevance_reason: 本文研究复杂网络中的中心结构假设检验问题，使用邻接谱半径作为检验统计量来识别网络中的中心结构。这与LLM压缩、量化、剪枝、蒸馏或任何模型压缩主题完全无关，属于网络科学/图论领域。应予以硬门控。

title: Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.

title: MERIT: Scaling KG Foundation Models with Relation Transformers
abstract: Knowledge graph (KG) foundation models (KGFMs) predict links on unseen graphs zero-shot. KGFMs have been pioneered by ULTRA which builds a relation graph from co-occurrences that match motif templates, and passes messages over it to obtain relation representations. More recent KGFMs such as MOTIF and TRIX increase the size of this relation graph, and FLOCK replaces message-passing with probabilistic random-walk ensembles. However, larger relation graphs mean more messages, and more walks mean more sequences to encode, so they improve performance at higher training and inference cost. This cost hinders their use in more complex reasoning tasks, such as complex query answering. To reverse this trend, we design MERIT, the first KGFM with a transformer relation encoder: every relation name attends to every other, and the motifs enter as a soft prior rather than as edges. Over 56 benchmarks, MERIT matches the zero-shot MRR of SoTA KGFMs while being 6x faster than TRIX and over 100x faster than FLOCK at inference. Fine-tuned for complex query answering like UltraQuery, MERITQuery improves over it at matched cost.

title: The Price of Precision: A Calibrated Cost Model for Mixed-Precision LLM Serving
abstract: Choosing a mixed-precision configuration for large language model (LLM) serving trades speed against accuracy. Allocators that use average bit-width or a memory budget as a speed proxy can miss changes in the resource that limits execution. We argue that served speed can be limited by compute, weight loading, or key-value (KV) cache access, depending on the phase, batch size, and context length. A byte-based proxy does not capture all of these costs, so fewer bits do not always mean faster serving. To address this gap, we build a cost model that accounts for the binding resource and use it in two ways. First, as a predictor: given a configuration and operating point, it estimates serving latency using constants calibrated for the model, GPU, and serving stack. We evaluate its accuracy across three hardware classes. Second, as an allocator: we combine modeled time costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs and use a dynamic program to select a configuration under a latency or accuracy budget. We compare its configurations against byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.

title: Robust Detection of Directional Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks for Radiological Imaging
abstract: Deep learning is now central to radiology, helping detect changes on X-rays, CTs, and MRIs. However, these systems are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks - small, crafted perturbations that mislead models while appearing unchanged to humans. Such errors risk missed cancers or false positives. Studies show over 90% attack success on medical scans. Almost 30% of US hospitals use AI in imaging in 2023. Thus, an effective method of detecting such attacks and their directionality is crucial to ensure the credibility and reliability of medical systems based on DNNs. We propose a novel detection framework that leverages subsequent attacks using random noise to identify adversarial perturbations. Our approach uses the analysis of variations in the Sigmoid function to distinguish genuine medical images from adversarially manipulated ones. Specifically, we compare prediction differences between clean and attacked images, as well as between different adversarially altered versions, to improve detection accuracy. We evaluated our method on three popular medical datasets including 'Chest X-Ray Images for Classification', 'Retinal Fundus Multi-disease Image Dataset' and 'Brain Tumor Dataset' under various attack scenarios, including random noise. Our framework achieved up to 99.8% ACC in identifying adversarial directional attacks, significantly outperforming existing defense mechanisms. It consistently identified adversarial samples across varying attack strengths while keeping false positives low, showing strong reliability and potential for clinical use. Furthermore, our proposal highlights its potential for real-world deployment.

title: Adaptive Role Assignment and Controlled Feature Reconstruction for Federated Image Semantic Communication
abstract: Hybrid federated semantic communication enables user equipment (UEs) to contribute model updates or semantic features under a shared training framework. However, heterogeneous role costs and the interaction between model aggregation and feature reconstruction (FR) remain key challenges in practical radio access network (RAN) deployment. To address these issues, we propose ARC-FedSC, a RAN-aware framework that coordinates UE role assignment and server-side controlled FR under a fixed communication budget. Within ARC-FedSC, RAN Aware Role-Bandit learns the historical contribution of UEs in different roles together with current uplink conditions, while Temporal Consistency Alignment (TCA) regulates FR according to recent model aggregation directions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 with time-varying RAN channels show that ARC-FedSC outperforms baselines across all five tested role configurations in the later training stage, with the best configurations achieving about 24.17 dB average PSNR over the last 20 rounds. Component level results further show that Role-Bandit maintains an average rolling UE coverage of 85.3%, compared with about 65.7% for baseline, while TCA reduces the probability of harmful FR events from 0.245 to 0.093, corresponding to a 62.0% reduction. Ablation and sensitivity studies further support the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed design.

title: Screening Collapse under Recursive Synthetic Data
abstract: Recursive synthetic-data training can degrade a fitted model, but its effects on the variable-screening stage that precedes model fitting are less understood. When each generation labels data for the next, a marginal screener ranks variables against the current pseudo-label target rather than the original response. Across generations, this target drift can erode or reverse the active--inactive score margin and cause screening to discard variables that clean-label screening would retain. We call this process \emph{screening collapse}. In a Gaussian linear model with minimum-norm recursive generators, we establish finite-sample screening bounds, characterize a late-generation information-loss limit, and derive a minimax impossibility result. Screening collapse can precede and compound ordinary model collapse: omitted variables incur a covariance-weighted loss that no refit restricted to the selected variables can eliminate, while recursive labels further degrade estimation on the retained variables. We also examine two approaches to mitigating screening collapse. Fixed-fraction real-label retention preserves a clean-label component but leaves resolution fixed, whereas data accumulation can avoid screening collapse if the pooled target preserves a positive margin and the growing sample resolves it. Numerical experiments on gene-expression data support the theoretical findings.

title: ProML: Progressive Multi-label Learning
abstract: Multi-label learning typically pursues model construction through the joint optimization of label fitting, correlation modeling, and structural regularization. While empirically effective, such a coupled paradigm imposes multiple learning objectives on a single predictive parameter matrix, forcing it to simultaneously fit observed labels and encode structural priors. This coupling may induce ill-conditioned optimization geometry, increase hyper-parameter sensitivity, and complicate capacity control. To address the these issues, this paper proposes a Progressive Multi-Label Learning (ProML) framework, which decouples direct label fitting from predictor learning via the introduction of an auxiliary predictive variable. This auxiliary variable admits a closed-form solution, yielding an equivalent profiled objective in which the supervised fitting term is scaled by a trade-off parameter. This result provides a unified view of ProML and conventional coupled learning, with the latter recovered as a limiting case. We theoretically analyze the optimization geometry of ProML and show that, under quadratic positive semidefinite structural regularization, ProML attenuates the dominant curvature of the fitting term, enlarges the stable learning rate range, and provides a controllable fidelity-regularization trade-off. Further, we instantiate the ProML for multi-label feature selection task by integrating global-local label priors and row-sparse regularization. Extensive experiments and controlled optimization analyses on 12 benchmark datasets empirically corroborate the theoretical analysis and demonstrate the robust and competitive performance of the proposed method.

title: Joint Contrastive-Adversarial Representation Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
abstract: Effective unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) requires a representation that captures transferable structure from both the labeled source domain and the unlabeled target domain. We introduce Joint Contrastive-Adversarial Representation Learning (JCAR), a two-stage framework that learns a common representation from the union of unlabeled source and target samples by combining contrastive learning with adversarial domain alignment, and then freezes the representation to fit a source-supervised predictor. We establish a non-asymptotic excess-risk bound for this procedure that couples representation and domain-discriminator estimation while separating downstream prediction, with explicit neural-network approximation errors. Under the stated assumptions and common Hölder smoothness $β\geq1$, the bound identifies a sufficiently large unlabeled-sample regime in which the downstream rate is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^{-β/(2β+d)})$, where $m$ counts labeled source samples and logarithmic factors are suppressed. The labeled-sample exponent is governed by the latent dimension $d$ rather than the ambient dimension $p$, which enters the pretraining cost. Experiments on Office-31, Office-Home, and DomainNet demonstrate clear transfer gains across diverse domain shifts, with particularly strong performance when representations are learned from scratch.

title: An Attention-Guided Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Boundary Integral Computation in Physical Field Reconstruction
abstract: In practical engineering and scientific computing, a real physical system can be reduced to a boundary value problem, and the adequate boundary information to determine the interior spatial distribution and evolutionary state of the physical field can be solved with linear equations, alternatively, the the real physical problem can be treated with boundary problems with in adequate information problems in field of machine learning. This paper proposes a deep learning framework for the recovery of missing boundary information using an attention-guided graph neural network (GNN) surrogate. The framework extracts features from the physical information on the discretized boundary into a latent space, and the missing boundary quantities are then predicted by the network. Thus, the nonlinear mapping from known boundary quantities to missing boundary quantities is learned using a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture, while an attention mechanism is incorporated to better model the correlations among different types of boundary information. Furthermore, the interior physical field can be reconstructed using the conventional boundary element method (BEM) integral formulation. The effectiveness of the GNN-BEM framework is evaluated using numerical examples of the two-dimensional Laplace and Poisson equations, which demonstrate good performance in reconstruction accuracy, local detail preservation, and model stability. The results show that GNN-BEM provides a feasible computational framework for boundary information recovery and fast interior physical field reconstruction for partial differential equations under complex boundary conditions.

title: The Gradient That Top-k Distillation Never Computes
abstract: Many deployed distillation pipelines show the student a truncated view of the teacher: keep the top-k probabilities, renormalize, and minimize a divergence on what remains. Renormalization is assumed to account for the missing mass. We prove that it removes the visibility of tail mass, not the freedom to move it. The renormalized objective depends only on log-odds among the retained tokens, so at each position its gradient along the directions that control tail mass is exactly zero; on a real teacher that component measures $2$-$3\times10^{-15}$ of the gradient. The full-vocabulary gradient equals the truncated gradient plus a residual weighted by the tail masses, and training acts only on the first term. Without the cross-entropy term, a top-k student's tail mass drifts away from the teacher's while a full-vocabulary control moves slightly toward it; with it, the gap shrinks about fourfold but persists. On seven open-weight teachers, the retained set determines the teacher's distribution only from $k=d+1$ ($d$ the hidden dimension): recovery is exact from there on all seven, and commonly cached sizes sit below it. In our off-policy runs the practical effect is real but smaller than the choice of teacher-student pair. Renormalization is a normalization, not a safeguard. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/top-k-distillation.

title: Towards Robust Calibration Dataset for Domain-General Mixture of Experts Pruning
abstract: Post-training expert pruning is a promising deployment technique for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The calibration set is an integral part of the pruning process, however, its correlation with evaluation performance is largely misunderstood and unintuitive. In this work, we present an empirical study of the robustness of calibration perturbations, specifically in MoE models. Showing how calibration size, language, and data distribution affect layer-wise expert pruning for gpt-oss-20b. Our findings reveal that (1) domain-general pruning quality receives minimal benefit from scaling calibration data beyond small sample sizes, (2) cross-lingual calibration transfers effectively, with English-only calibration maintaining strong performance across seven languages of varying typologies and scripts, and (3) a diverse calibration data resembling the pretraining distribution can yield comparable or superior performance to test-distribution data. Ultimately, we provide practical insights as a recipe for better understanding calibration for more effective domain-general expert pruning.

title: The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps
abstract: Structural pruning followed by a recovery stage is the standard recipe for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet the two stages are typically designed and tuned in isolation. In this work, we study how their interaction shapes the compressed model, sweeping ordering, the data that drives each stage, and the alignment of their training objectives. We find that instruction-following is the first capability to collapse under pruning, well before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling, and that much of the pruning in-domain loss is likely not knowledge loss but a domain-agnostic failure to respond coherently to the prompt. We find in our setting that in-domain data is the strongest pruning signal, whereas instruction-style data recovers the most. Stage order matters little, but only marginally. We further analyze how the importance ranking drifts before and after pruning. Together these results give practitioners a concrete recipe for composing pruning and recovery.

title: Latent-Space Importance Weighting under Covariate Shift
abstract: In this work, we propose a transfer learning algorithm for covariate shift, integrating sample reweighting with representation learning. A key feature of our approach is the use of a lower-dimensional latent space for modeling, in contrast to conventional methods that operate directly in the high-dimensional ambient space. Our method estimates the density ratio of learned latent features for downstream weighted prediction. We establish explicit target-domain excess-risk rates with independent data folds for strictly sufficient learned representations with regular learned-space prediction scores and density ratios. We give dimension comparisons under stated smoothness conditions and a variance comparison for true weights and a fixed predictor. General finite-sample inequalities retain representation-quality errors. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate gains from combining learned representations and latent weighting, and reveal sensitivity to initialization and domain choice.

title: Truncation Samplers Are Nested: Comparing Decoding Rules Is a Measurement Problem
abstract: Settling one comparison between two truncation samplers has cost six thousand A100-hours, and nothing says in advance how far apart two samplers can be. We observe that almost every deployed truncation rule keeps a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, so any two such rules are nested at every decoding step. Nesting yields a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which both samplers emit identical text until they first disagree. Accumulated over a generation, this gives a separation certificate that bounds the difference between two samplers on any bounded outcome, is computable from logs a comparison already produces, and equals their sequence-level total variation distance exactly when neither rule ever overtakes the other. Two consequences follow without measurement: exactness is fragile, and certifying a small difference requires the two retained masses to agree to very high precision at every step. On six open-weight models over four math and science benchmarks, the certificate for every hyperparameter grid we tested is at least 0.998, so a bound alone rarely settles a comparison, although two members of one family can be far closer. What remains useful is the coupling, which gives an unbiased paired estimator that cuts variance $1.2$-$3.8\times$ against prompt-level pairing. Read against benchmark sizes at the default pair's variance and our point estimate of its between-prompt component, resolving a one-point difference needs 8 to 32 samples per prompt on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond and about 210 on AIME 2025; at that component's upper confidence bound GPQA-Diamond needs more than 32 and AIME 2025 cannot be resolved at any sample count. Choosing a truncation sampler is a measurement problem at least as much as a design one. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/truncation-samplers.

title: UNISON: A Unified Framework for Learning from Scored Bags
abstract: We introduce UNISON, a unified framework that bridges multiple instance learning and recommendation systems by treating both as instances of learning from scored bag collections of (item, score) pairs. Unlike traditional approaches that address bag-level classification and personalized recommendation as separate problems, UNISON decomposes learning into three interconnected stages: (1) learning universal item representations, (2) modeling bag-specific preference patterns through lightweight personalized parameters, and (3) inferring bag-level characteristics from learned preferences. We justify the architectural choice of linear bag-specific scoring through a first-order analysis: when item embeddings are sufficiently smooth in the score, a linear function approximates the score up to a Taylor remainder controlled by the curvature of the underlying preference function. For cold-start scenarios, we show that the cold-bag fitting problem reduces to ridge-less linear regression with a closed-form solution, and provide convergence guarantees for the iterative variant. Empirically, UNISON matches or outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse domains: entertainment (books, movies), immunology (T cell receptor (TCR) based classification), and microbiome, offering superior computational efficiency and interpretability. A controlled synthetic experiment further confirms that the bag-specific parameters ($w_j, b_j$) recover the latent factors that drive item scores even when the projection $φ$ has no access to the original scoring mechanism (AUC > 0.998). UNISON is available at https://github.com/louzounlab/UNISON.

title: Vision-Predictor-Action: Towards Efficient Embodied AI via Neuro-Symbolic JEPA Predictors
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly generate robot actions token by token through Large Language Model (LLM) decoders, causing inference latency to grow with action sequence length and limiting closed-loop control frequency. We present Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces autoregressive decoders with a lightweight latent control loop. A shared vision encoder and a frozen text encoder embed observations, goal images, and instructions; a neuro-symbolic selector chooses a discrete skill; a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor forecasts the next latent state; and a flow-matching solver generates an entire action chunk in a few integration steps, so that sequential network evaluations per decision step do not depend on the action horizon. We analyze inference complexity, regularization against representation collapse, and conditions under which latent sub-goal thresholding limits error accumulation across task phases. As an initial proof of concept, we evaluated VPA on the LIBERO-10 suite. The trainable model has under 20M parameters (checkpoint under 75 MB, excluding a frozen 63.4M-parameter CLIP text encoder); a decision step of a single-camera reference configuration takes 10-14 ms on an Apple M4; and trained only on LIBERO-10 demonstrations in under three hours on a single GPU, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes. These preliminary results from a single training run suggest the approach is workable. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/ylee-sling/Vision-Predictor-Action and https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/vpa-libero10, and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960920.

title: ELECT: Settling Identity Before Rendering for Scalable Story Visualization
abstract: Training-free story visualization without reference images must preserve recurring entities across frames while scaling to long narratives. Existing methods typically maintain consistency by conditioning each frame on other frames of the same story, coupling generation time, VRAM, or both to story length. We introduce ELECT, which instead settles cross-frame identity before final rendering through a language-guided scene-entity mapping and stationary anchors elected from the model's own drafts. This makes the per-frame cost of the final rendering pass independent of story length. Joint attention exceeds 96 GB of VRAM at 32 scenes, whereas ELECT remains at 8.3 s per frame and under 20 GB VRAM from 10 to 1000 scenes. On the Story50 long-story benchmark, ELECT reaches 0.833 average Character Consistency Similarity (aCCS), compared with 0.826 for ten-round refinement, at one seventh of its generation cost, with lower text alignment (0.327 vs. 0.340). At 1000 scenes, to our knowledge, the first evaluation of training-free story visualization at this length, ELECT exceeds ten-round refinement by 0.017 aCCS and the nearest flat-cost baseline by 0.091, while also surpassing refinement in text alignment at one twenty-fourth of its generation time. These results show that long-horizon consistency need not require increasingly expensive inter-frame conditioning as stories grow.

title: An Interpretable Linguistically-Grounded Analysis of Scene Saliency in Movie Screenplays
abstract: We investigate the factors affecting salience in movie screenplay by posing two research questions: 1. {\em Does Uniform Information Density (UID) predict salient scenes?} 2. {\em What other linguistic properties distinguish salient scenes from non-salient background?} We answer both questions through a controlled corpus study on the MENSA corpus, paired with a Linguistically-Grounded Salience Model (LGSM), a dual-stream classifier that fuses a frozen BERT encoder with explicit linguistic features through adaptive gating. The UID picture is layered in long-form discourse. Per-scene UID summaries carry no independent signal once length is controlled, but at the token level salient scenes match non-salient material in the bulk while specifically suppressing the rarest, hardest-to-predict tokens in the upper tail. UID therefore lives at the within-scene token level rather than as a per-scene aggregate. Salient scenes also show a moderate and sustained cast of central characters (following an inverted-U pattern), strong third-person usage, syntactically simpler language, and more abstract vocabulary about motivation and conflict. LGSM exploits this signature and improves recall on salient scenes over a strong semantic baseline while yielding better downstream summaries.

title: Beyond Aggregate Drift: Optimal Client-Specific Windows in Federated Learning
abstract:
We study federated learning from continuously arriving data: each client samples from its own distribution, these distributions drift over time, and the server must track the minimizer of the clients' weighted average loss. Clients are not alike as they collect data at different rates, with different noise, and change at different speeds. The main question is how much history should each one keep? A single shared window must serve every client at once, and so makes a fast-changing client carry the sampling noise of a slow, nearly stationary one.
  We give each client a memory of its own, sized to that client's noise, arrival rate, and drift, and refresh it by restarted accelerated method that starts from a common point. The tracking error is then bounded by \[
  R\left(\sum_m w_m^{3/2}\,σ_m\sqrt{γ_m/λ_m}\right)^{2/3}, \] for clients with weight $w_m$, noise $σ_m$, arrival rate $λ_m$, and drift rate $γ_m$ on a domain of diameter $R$. This is never worse than what any common window can achieve, and strictly better whenever noise and drift are spread unevenly across clients.
  A lower bound that puts different groups of clients on different drift clocks shows this quantity is the right one. The two bounds agree up to a constant whenever the clients occupy boundedly many refresh scales, and in general differ only by the sixth root of the number of scales. Experiments show the gain comes from the memory rather than from the solver: it persists across accelerated, stochastic-gradient, and one-step methods, and against a separately tuned common-memory baseline.

title: Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners
abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.
